1291.event_title: Nietzsche’s marriage proposal to Lou Salomé is refused
1291.event: In 1882, at the writer Malwida von Meysenbug’s salon in Rome, the philosophers Friedrich Nietzsche and Paul Rée met Lou Salomé, a brilliant young Russian student. Both men fell in love with her, but she turned down their proposals of marriage and suggested instead that the three live and study together; apart from three weeks sharing an apartment in Leipzig, the plan came to nothing. After Nietzsche’s unsuccessful proposal, Salomé and Rée left together for Berlin, and the friendship ended painfully for him.
1291.explanation: Nietzsche gave his heart completely while Salomé kept hers firmly her own.
1291.tie_back: The kural’s speaker complains that the beloved’s heart stays loyal to him alone while her own heart runs off to him; Nietzsche’s heart went to Salomé while hers remained entirely her own.
1291._accuracy_note: Reasonable: one heart given away while the other stays self-possessed matches the kural’s complaint, but this was an unreturned courtship, not a quarrel inside a marriage.

1292.event_title: Mary Wollstonecraft travels to Scandinavia on Gilbert Imlay’s business
1292.event: In Paris during the French Revolution, Mary Wollstonecraft lived with the American adventurer Gilbert Imlay and in 1794 gave birth to their daughter, Fanny, but he soon drifted away from her. In 1795, after a Norwegian captain had made off with a valuable silver cargo from one of Imlay’s ships, Imlay asked her to go to Scandinavia to recover it, and she set out in June with her baby and a maid, spending more than three months negotiating with officials and travelling. She wrote letters to Imlay throughout, and on returning to London found that he had taken up with another woman; the letters became her book Letters Written During a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark (1796).
1292.explanation: Even after Imlay had made clear how little he valued her, Wollstonecraft went far out of her way for him and kept writing to him.
1292.tie_back: The kural’s wife tells her heart that even after seeing he does not care, it still goes to him, assuming he will not be angry; Wollstonecraft’s journey and letters show a heart that kept going toward a man who had stopped caring.
1292._accuracy_note: Strong fit for a heart that keeps going to a man it has seen no longer cares, though the journey was also undertaken on business; the Scandinavian journey, the letters to Imlay and the book are confirmed by the Public Domain Review, a British travel-writing scholarly source and Britannica.

1293.event_title: Emma Hamilton dies in debt and exile at Calais
1293.event: On the morning of the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805, Admiral Lord Nelson added a codicil to his will asking the British government to provide for Emma Hamilton, but the government, which gave money and honours to Nelson’s family, ignored her. Deep in debt, she had to sell Nelson’s house at Merton and her mementoes of him, and in 1813 she was arrested for debt and lived within the bounds of the King’s Bench debtors’ prison, cut off by many people she had once entertained lavishly. She fled abroad to escape her creditors and died at Calais on 15 January 1815.
1293.explanation: Once Nelson was gone and her fortunes collapsed, the society and state that had celebrated her abandoned her.
1293.tie_back: The kural quotes the saying that the ruined have no friends, and Emma Hamilton’s last years are a textbook case of friends vanishing once misfortune struck.
1293._accuracy_note: Strong for the proverb the kural quotes, though the kural uses it of a wife deserted by her own heart rather than by society.

1294.event_title: Gustav Mahler walks with Sigmund Freud in Leiden
1294.event: In July 1910 the composer Gustav Mahler, then fifty and at the height of his fame, discovered that his wife Alma had become romantically involved with the young architect Walter Gropius. In August he travelled to Leiden in the Netherlands to consult Sigmund Freud, who came by tram from his holiday at Noordwijk aan Zee. The two men talked for about four hours while walking through the city; Mahler died nine months later.
1294.explanation: Faced with the threat of losing Alma, Mahler did not break with her but sought to understand his own feelings and keep the marriage.
1294.tie_back: The kural’s wife complains that her heart will not first sulk and then enjoy the making-up; Mahler, instead of turning his hurt into a quarrel, put his effort into holding on to the one he loved.
1294._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows a wounded spouse unwilling to stage a lasting quarrel, but the sources record the consultation, not Mahler’s inner reasoning, and the situation is far more serious than a lovers’ sulk.

1295.event_title: Mary Livingstone rejoins David Livingstone on the Zambezi
1295.place: Shupanga (Chupanga), on the Zambezi River, Mozambique
1295.event: Mary Moffat married the missionary-explorer David Livingstone in 1845 and travelled with him on many journeys in southern Africa, until in 1852 he sent her and their four children back to Britain for their health and safety. She lived there in near poverty during his long years of exploration. Determined to return to Africa with him, she joined his Zambezi expedition in 1862 but caught malaria and died at Shupanga in April 1862.
1295.explanation: Mary Livingstone suffered first from long separation and then, when reunited, lost her husband again within months through her own death.
1295.tie_back: The kural’s heart fears not having the beloved when he is away and fears parting when he is near, and Mary Livingstone’s story moved from years of separation to a reunion that was itself cut short.
1295._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the pattern of separation and brief reunion fits, but the sources do not record Mary’s own fears, which are the heart of the kural.

1296.event_title: Mary Shelley begins her Journal of Sorrow
1296.event: In the summer of 1822 the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley and his friend Edward Williams drowned when their boat sank in a storm while sailing to Lerici in Italy. Left a widow at twenty-four, Mary Shelley began a new journal on 2 October 1822, later known as her Journal of Sorrow, addressing the blank page as the confidant to whom she could pour out her innermost thoughts. Her only regular companions at this time were her young son, Percy Florence, and the journal itself.
1296.explanation: Alone with her memories, Mary Shelley turned her grief inward onto the page, where it could be expressed but not escaped.
1296.tie_back: The kural’s wife says that whenever she sat alone and thought of her husband, her own heart seemed ready to devour her, which matches Mary Shelley’s solitary, grieving journal.
1296._accuracy_note: Reasonable: solitary thoughts of an absent husband turning into torment fit well, though the kural describes temporary separation and pique, not widowhood.

1297.event_title: Lady Caroline Lamb’s open pursuit of Lord Byron
1297.event: Early in 1812 Lady Caroline Lamb, wife of William Lamb (a future prime minister), read Lord Byron’s new poem Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage and wrote him an anonymous admiring letter. Their relationship that year became a public scandal: Byron’s friend John Cam Hobhouse said all London agreed she had set her heart on him, and Hobhouse barely prevented the two from eloping. In 1816 she published the novel Glenarvon, a thinly veiled account of the affair.
1297.explanation: Caroline Lamb’s feelings for Byron overrode every rule of reserve expected of a married woman of her class, and she paid for it with lasting notoriety.
1297.tie_back: The kural’s speaker says that, caught up with a heart that cannot forget her beloved, she has forgotten even her modesty, which is how London saw Caroline Lamb’s conduct in 1812.
1297._accuracy_note: Reasonable to strong for modesty forgotten through longing, but this was a scandalous relationship outside marriage, unlike the wedded love of the kural.

1298.event_title: Nadezhda Mandelstam memorises her husband’s poems
1298.event: The Russian poet Osip Mandelstam was arrested by Stalin’s police in 1934 and again in May 1938, and died later that year in a transit prison camp near Vladivostok. His wife, Nadezhda, committed his poems to memory in the hope that one day she could publish them, and she eventually did. She later wrote the memoir Hope Against Hope, which records their life together and preserves his memory.
1298.explanation: Through years of danger and loss, Nadezhda Mandelstam chose to carry her husband’s best qualities, his poetry, in her own mind.
1298.tie_back: The kural says the loving heart, rather than scorning the beloved, dwells on his good qualities, and Nadezhda Mandelstam devoted her life to holding on to her husband’s finest work.
1298._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for a heart that holds on to the beloved's best qualities, though in the kural this happens during a lovers' quarrel rather than after loss; the arrests, the memorised poems and the memoir are confirmed by the Posen Library and an EBSCO reference article.

1299.event_title: Viktor Frankl holds on to the image of his wife in the camps
1299.event: The Viennese psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was deported with his family in 1942 to Theresienstadt and in 1944 to Auschwitz; his wife later died at Bergen-Belsen. In his book Man’s Search for Meaning (1946) he described marching to a work site in the dark when a fellow prisoner whispered about their wives, and how his own mind then clung to his wife’s image with great vividness. He wrote that this inner image sustained him and taught him that love is the highest goal a person can aspire to.
1299.explanation: Stripped of everything else, Frankl found that what he carried in his own heart could still keep him company in suffering.
1299.tie_back: The kural asks who will stand by one in sorrow if one’s own heart will not; Frankl’s experience shows the other side of the same truth, a heart that did stand by him when nothing else could.
1299._accuracy_note: Reasonable: it shows one’s own heart as the essential companion in suffering, though it illustrates the kural from the positive side rather than the wife’s complaint about a disloyal heart.

1300.event: On 6 October 1802, in the village of Heiligenstadt outside Vienna, Ludwig van Beethoven wrote a long letter to his brothers Carl and Johann that has become known as the Heiligenstadt Testament. In it he explained that people who thought him unfriendly, stubborn or misanthropic misjudged him, because they did not know the secret cause of his behaviour, his growing deafness. He wrote that such experiences had brought him to the edge of despair.
1300.explanation: Beethoven’s own failing hearing cut him off from people, and the people around him, not knowing why, turned against him in their judgements.
1300.tie_back: The kural says that when even one’s own heart will not act like kin, it is no wonder strangers do not, and Beethoven found that when his own body failed him, outsiders also failed to understand him.
1300._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it pairs an inner failure with the indifference of others, but the inner failure is physical deafness, not a disloyal heart, and the setting is not romantic love.
